opus-5.5.text:
I think takedown papers can be really valuable, but it depends a lot on the spirit in which they're written. At their best, they're a form of scientific hygiene. Our field moves incredibly fast, and many results get published, cited, and built on before anyone has carefully checked whether they hold up under different conditions, with stronger baselines, or with more careful hyperparameter tuning. A good takedown paper slows things down for a moment and asks: do we actually know what we think we know?

The most useful ones I've seen don't just say "this is wrong." They explain *why* the original result appeared to work. Maybe the baseline was undertuned, maybe the evaluation leaked information, maybe the effect only shows up at small scale. That's scientifically interesting in its own right. Understanding why something looked true is often as informative as the original claim, because it tells the whole community which pitfalls to watch for.

I've been on both sides of this. With the lottery ticket work, people pushed back, found settings where the original procedure didn't work, especially at larger scale, and that pushback was genuinely helpful. It forced us to understand the phenomenon better, and it led to the work on rewinding and on linear mode connectivity and stability. I'd much rather someone find the limits of my ideas than have the field build a tower on a foundation nobody checked.

Where takedown papers go wrong is when they become about dunking on people rather than about understanding. If the tone is adversarial or the goal is to embarrass someone, it makes people defensive, it discourages others from publishing bold or exploratory ideas, and it turns science into a status contest. It also matters to be fair: test the claim the authors actually made, in the setting they made it, before showing where it breaks.

So my ideal is a culture where these papers are seen as normal and even collegial, part of the conversation rather than an attack. Reproducing and stress-testing results should be rewarded, not treated as second-class work. Honestly, I'd love it if more of us invited this kind of scrutiny of our own papers. That's how a field actually accumulates knowledge rather than just accumulating publications.

r001.rationale: The response praises takedown papers and says they help the field accumulate knowledge, but it does not claim that producing only such papers does little to build knowledge.

r002.rationale: It calls for carefully checking claims and stress-testing results, but does not say a takedown paper should establish a standard for future papers to meet.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because the lottery ticket work ended up being on the receiving end of some of this, and I've also written things that were, let's say, less than flattering about other people's results. And my honest view is that takedown papers are one of the most valuable things a field can produce, with some caveats.

The reason is pretty simple. Our field has an enormous incentive to produce positive results. You get a paper accepted when you show something works. You get a lot less credit for showing something doesn't work, or that something works for a much more boring reason than the authors claimed. So we end up with this accumulation of claims that nobody has really pressure-tested, and then people build on them, and then three years later you discover the foundation was sand. A good takedown paper is the field's immune system. It's somebody saying, wait, let's actually check this.

The caveat is about how you do it. The takedowns I find useful are the ones that are really careful and really generous about the original work. They say, here's the claim as stated, here's what we tried, here's exactly where it holds and where it breaks. That's science. The ones I find less useful are the ones that are mostly about the authors rather than the claim, or that cherry-pick a setting where something fails and declare the whole thing dead. That's not a takedown, that's a different kind of overclaiming, and it's just as damaging.

The other thing I'd say is that the best takedowns usually aren't purely negative. The most useful one for me personally was the "Rethinking the Value of Network Pruning" line of work, which really challenged some of the lottery ticket story at scale. It was uncomfortable. But it forced us to be much more precise about what we were actually claiming, and the follow-up work on rewinding and stability came directly out of trying to understand where they were right. So the takedown didn't kill the idea. It sharpened it. I think that's the ideal outcome, where the original authors and the critics both end up understanding the phenomenon better than either did before.

And I'd love for the field to make this a normal thing to do, something you can build a reputation on, rather than a thing that feels like picking a fight. Because right now a lot of the replication and negative-result work happens informally, on Twitter or in reading groups, and it never makes it into the record. If we want our results to be trustworthy, we need the critique to be as citable as the claim.

r001.rationale: The response praises takedown papers and argues they help pressure-test claims, but does not say that producing only takedown papers would do little to build scientific knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response calls for careful, fair critiques and more citable negative results, but does not say takedown papers should establish a scientific standard for future papers to meet.

astra-6.text:
I think a good takedown paper should leave us understanding something better, not just believing in something less. If you show that a result doesn’t hold, that’s useful. But the really interesting question is why. Was there a problem with the experimental setup? Was the baseline too weak? Does the claim hold in a narrower set of circumstances than we thought?

That’s a contribution because it gives the field somewhere to go. You’re not just saying, “These people were wrong.” You’re saying, “Here’s a better way to run this experiment, or here’s the distinction we need to make.” And I think you have to give the original work a fair shot. Make the strongest version of the argument you’re criticizing, and then see what survives. The goal should be to improve our collective understanding, not to win an argument.

r001.rationale: The response says a good takedown paper should improve understanding, but does not assert that producing only takedown papers does little to build scientific knowledge.

r002.rationale: It suggests better experiments and useful distinctions, but does not argue that a takedown paper should establish a scientific standard for future papers to meet.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a good takedown paper can be incredibly valuable if it leaves us understanding something better. If the conclusion is just, “These people are wrong,” that’s less interesting to me than, “Here’s the assumption that breaks, here’s when it breaks, and here’s what that tells us about the problem.”

You should also take the strongest version of the work seriously. Give it a fair shot. If you can explain why an idea looked promising and then show precisely where it falls short, you’ve given the field something to build on. And sometimes you discover that the idea works in a narrower setting than people thought. That’s progress, too.

The distinction for me is whether you’re trying to win an argument or help us figure out what’s true. You can be very direct and very critical while still doing the latter.

r001.rationale: The response says a takedown paper is more valuable when it improves understanding, but does not assert that producing only takedown papers does little to build scientific knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response recommends explaining where an idea falls short and giving the field something to build on, but does not say a takedown paper should establish a standard for future papers to meet.
